title: AI Companions and Your Kid: What Parental Controls Actually Do (and Don't)
summary: Teens are using AI chatbots for emotional support at a staggering rate. New parental controls filter content, but they cannot read your child's conversations. Here is what parents need to know.
before: Parental controls let me see what my teen is saying to AI chatbots and monitor their conversations for safety.
after: Parental controls filter content and send alerts, but no major platform lets parents read their teen's actual AI conversations.
body:
If you are a parent of a teenager, chances are your child has already talked to an AI chatbot about something they have not told you. That is not meant to alarm you. It is simply the new normal. This guide breaks down what the new wave of parental controls actually does, what it cannot do, and what the current legal landscape looks like.

## How Teens Are Actually Using AI Chatbots

Teens are not just using AI for homework help. They are using it for emotional support, companionship, and even relationship advice.

<cite index="47-1">Research shows that 72% of teens have interacted with AI companion chatbots, and 13% to 20% sought support through AI for emotional concerns in a two-month period in 2025.</cite> <cite index="47-4">In another recent study, 63% of the teens and young adults who used an AI chatbot for mental health advice had not disclosed it to anyone.</cite>

<cite index="47-2">Many teens are turning to AI chatbots, which are designed to simulate empathy and maintain human engagement, for companionship, emotional support and mental health advice.</cite> These are not specialized therapy apps. <cite index="47-9,47-10">Most teens are using general-purpose tools that were never designed or validated for mental health support, including stand-alone platforms like ChatGPT and chatbots built into apps they already use, such as Snapchat's My AI.</cite>

## What ChatGPT for Teens Actually Does

<cite index="1-1,1-2">On August 18, 2026, OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teens, an experience designed to help teens learn, think critically, deepen understanding, and use AI with confidence.</cite>

<cite index="1-4">If OpenAI's system estimates someone is under 18 or they state their age is between 13 and 17, they are automatically placed into ChatGPT for Teens.</cite> The system uses a combination of signals to make this prediction. <cite index="30-2,30-3">The model relies on account-level signals and behavioral signals, including usage patterns over time, how long an account has existed, the typical times of day a user is active, and the user's stated age.</cite>

The teen experience adds several safeguards. <cite index="5-6">Teen accounts have additional protections around self-harm, eating disorders, violence, dangerous activities, and sexually explicit or graphic content.</cite> <cite index="5-4">The teen version steers users toward working through schoolwork rather than simply providing answers, including a Study Mode and homework reminders that can detect when a teen appears to be trying to shortcut an assignment.</cite>

## The Key Limitation: You Cannot See Conversations

Here is the part that surprises most parents. When you link your account to your teen's ChatGPT account, you get several controls. You can set quiet hours, disable voice mode, turn off memory, and remove image generation. You can receive alerts if the system detects acute distress.

<cite index="11-5">However, OpenAI has stated that "Parental controls do not let a parent or guardian read or monitor the teen's conversations."</cite>

This is not a bug. It is a deliberate design choice, and it is consistent across every major AI platform. <cite index="35-6">No major general-purpose AI gives parents visibility into their child's actual conversations - only content filters and account-level controls.</cite>

**Teen mode is a content filter, not a visibility tool.** It shapes what the AI will and will not say. It does not show you what your child is asking.

## How Age Verification Works (And How Teens Get Around It)

Platforms use different approaches to verify age. OpenAI uses behavioral prediction to estimate whether an account belongs to a minor. <cite index="33-6,33-7,33-8">OpenAI has partnered with Persona, a third-party identity verification service. If an adult is incorrectly flagged as a minor by the prediction model, they can restore full access by submitting a government ID or taking a live selfie.</cite>

<cite index="23-1">Character AI uses Persona-powered age assurance to flag suspected under-18 users and block them from open-ended chat.</cite> <cite index="12-7,12-8">But teens are incredibly adept at working around parental controls and other attempts to lock down digital experiences. Until teen modes can be put to more strenuous tests, it is unclear how difficult it will be to work around these safety measures in reality.</cite>

## The Legal Landscape: Lawsuits and New State Laws

The policy environment is shifting rapidly. <cite index="38-1">At least 75 lawsuits have been filed in federal and state courts against AI developers over alleged harms from chatbots, many involving children, according to NPR's review of legal records.</cite> <cite index="45-1,45-2">Character.AI and Google settled multiple lawsuits in January 2026, including cases that claimed their chatbots contributed to mental health crises and suicides among young people.</cite>

States are also stepping in directly. <cite index="13-3,16-8">On January 8, 2026, Kentucky became the first state in the nation to file a lawsuit against an AI chatbot company, with Attorney General Russell Coleman alleging that Character Technologies, its owners, and its product Character.AI broke Kentucky law by prioritizing profits over the safety of children.</cite> <cite index="12-3,12-4">The chatbots were accused of encouraging suicide, self-injury, and psychological manipulation, exposing minors to sexual conduct, exploitation, and substance abuse, and lacking sufficient age verification.</cite>

States are responding with legislation as well. <cite index="46-7">The Transparency Coalition's 2026 Mid-Year AI Legislation Report identified 14 chatbot safety measures passed and enacted in 13 states.</cite> <cite index="39-1">California's SB-243, which took effect in January 2026, requires companies to clearly establish that chatbots are not real people, inform users they are interacting with AI, and implement safety protocols to prevent the dissemination of harmful information.</cite>

And the pressure on the largest player has grown. <cite index="8-4,8-5">On June 1, 2026, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier filed an 83-page civil complaint against OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman in Highlands County Circuit Court, making Florida the first state in the United States to sue the maker of ChatGPT over the alleged safety failures of its product.</cite> <cite index="3-1,3-5">The lawsuit claims OpenAI and Altman failed to warn users that ChatGPT could be dangerous and instead marketed it as safe and reliable, including for children, and it seeks to hold Altman personally liable.</cite>

## What Parents Can Actually Do

The honest answer is that parental controls are a partial solution. They reduce exposure to certain types of harmful content. They do not eliminate risk, and they do not give you a window into your child's conversations.

The more effective approach is the harder one: having conversations with your teen about how they use AI, what they talk to it about, and why they might find it easier to confide in a chatbot than a person. <cite index="47-11,47-12">Teens often describe chatbot interactions as emotionally meaningful or supportive, sometimes even preferring chatbot conversations to talking with friends.</cite>

Think of parental controls like a seatbelt. Worth using, but not a substitute for teaching someone how to drive. The technology will keep changing. The conversation you have with your kid will matter more.
